text: Kafka isn't a message queue in the traditional sense — it's a durable, ordered log. Every event stays there for a configured retention period, readable by any number of independent consumers.
A traditional queue removes a message once consumed. Kafka's log keeps it — one consumer can read from the very beginning, another from wherever it left off, independently.

That one property — starting from any point in history — is what makes Kappa architecture actually work in practice. Reprocessing history means replaying the same log, not standing up a separate batch job.
A real Kafka deployment isn't an abstraction. It's a set of topics, each a named, partitioned log, visible in a real dashboard with live throughput and partition counts.
A durable log, not a disappearing queue — replay as the default. Next up: topics, partitions, and offsets.
